---
title: "Quiz: the journey of a drug through the cell"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
---

Follow the two routes from [the lecture](lec.qmd). Try each question before opening
the hint or answer. ELO tags show which mechanisms you are connecting.

---

**Q1.** A cell has many fluorescent LNP-labelled dots but little encoded protein.
Why does this not prove that translation is defective?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which side of the endosomal membrane can a ribosome reach? What exactly was labelled?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The label may be in **endosomes**, while the mRNA remains inaccessible to cytosolic
ribosomes. Lipid and RNA labels may also separate. Other possibilities include RNA
degradation or a later translation defect. Measure **cytosolic cargo access** and
**intact RNA**, then encoded protein; intracellular fluorescence alone does not
identify the failed step.
:::

---

**Q2.** Does delivered mRNA need to enter the nucleus to make a membrane antigen?
Where does translation begin, and what directs the protein into the ER?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Distinguish the route of the mRNA from the route of its growing protein.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No nuclear entry is required. Translation starts on a **cytosolic ribosome**.
An emerging **ER-targeting signal in the protein** is recognised by SRP, directing
the ribosome to an ER translocon. Translation and translocation continue together.
The mRNA's lipid carrier is not taken through the ER and Golgi with the antigen.
:::

---

**Q3.** A membrane antigen's glycosylated domain faces the ER lumen. Which side
will it face at the cell surface, and why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Do transport vesicles turn a membrane inside out?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The domain and its glycans face **outside the cell**. Budding and fusion preserve
orientation: ER lumen → carrier lumen → Golgi lumen → carrier lumen → extracellular
space. The cytosolic tail stays cytosolic. The protein does not flip across the
bilayer on the way.
:::

---

**Q4.** Give one way microtubules and one way ATP supply support this antigen's
journey. Why might a severe energy deficit affect several steps?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Think of carriers, motors, chaperones and pumps.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Microtubules are tracks for **motor-driven organelle and carrier movement**.
ATP powers motors and chaperones and supports pumps maintaining pH and calcium
stores; translation also requires energy. A severe deficit can therefore impair
translation, folding, transport and compartment conditions at once. Low surface
expression after ATP depletion does not isolate one delivery defect.
:::

---

**Q5.** Is a whole antigen at the plasma membrane the same as an antigen peptide
bound to MHC-I? Name one cellular process needed for each display.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Folded protein versus a short fragment of a protein.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. The **whole membrane antigen** is a folded protein delivered through the
secretory pathway. A **peptide–MHC-I complex** displays a short protein fragment;
the classical pathway uses proteasomal peptide generation, transport into the ER
and loading onto MHC-I before surface delivery. Antibody/B-cell recognition and
T-cell recognition use different structures. Signalling, costimulation and cell
context determine the response; this is a preview of Immunologi.
:::

---

**Q6.** Why can measuring total intracellular imatinib fail to predict kinase
inhibition? What additional measurement would help?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Is all measured drug freely available beside the kinase?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Total cellular drug includes material bound or sequestered away from its target;
the **free concentration at BCR–ABL1** may be different. A changed binding site
can also lower sensitivity. Add a **target-engagement assay** or a validated
kinase/phosphorylation readout, with total-protein and viability controls. A
phosphorylation readout measures pathway action, not direct binding by itself.
:::

---

**Q7.** Imatinib reduces a BCR–ABL1-dependent phosphorylation readout. Does that
prove the cells have undergone apoptosis? Explain how you would distinguish
arrest from death.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Separate molecular action, proliferation and cell fate.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. Pathway inhibition may cause **cell-cycle arrest**, apoptosis or persistence,
depending on the cell. Measure DNA synthesis or cell-cycle distribution to assess
proliferation, and use caspase activation together with appropriate viability or
membrane-integrity readouts to assess death. A lower cell count alone could reflect
slower division rather than increased death.
:::

---

**Q8.** A resistant cell has normal drug exposure but its BCR–ABL1 remains active.
Suggest a target-level explanation. How would a downstream bypass differ?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What can change at the kinase, and what can change after it?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A **kinase-domain mutation**, such as T315I in the imatinib example, can reduce
inhibitor sensitivity; increased target abundance is another possibility. Test
sequence, protein abundance and inhibitor sensitivity. With a **downstream
bypass**, the intended kinase could be inhibited while another route maintains
growth or survival. Compare target action with downstream signals and cell fate.
:::
